screens.title: Introduction to Test Doubles
screens.narratorSegment: In real systems your units rarely operate alone. When code under test depends on databases, networks, or third-party APIs, tests can become slow, flaky, or difficult to set up. Test doubles are a practical solution: lightweight stand-ins that let you control behavior and isolate the unit you want to verify. In this lesson you will learn the difference between data-focused doubles and interaction-focused doubles, and when to use an in-memory lightweight implementation. We will use a simple UserService example throughout — saving a user and sending a welcome email — so you can see concrete choices for each dependency. You will also learn common mistakes such as over-mocking and brittle verification, and how to choose the minimal double that gives you confidence without coupling tests to implementation details. By the end you will be able to pick between a stub, a mock, and a fake based on whether you care about the returned data, the interactions, or the dependency’s behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this first objectives panel we set clear, practical outcomes. First, you will explain the core problem that test doubles solve: dependencies make unit tests slow, brittle, or hard to set up, so doubles let you control and isolate behavior. Second, you'll differentiate between real dependencies and test doubles, learning the vocabulary so you can name what you replace and why. Third, you'll identify the core characteristics and use cases for stubs, mocks, and fakes — knowing when you need data, when you must assert an interaction, and when a lightweight implementation is appropriate. Fourth, you will understand the importance of test isolation: how keeping a single unit accountable prevents unrelated failures from cascading. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or visual cue so you remember whether you're testing for data, behavior, or behavior with simplified functionality.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives panel focuses on doing and avoiding mistakes. You will practice selecting the right double for a concrete example: a UserService that saves users and sends welcome emails. You will learn to choose stubs when a method must return a controlled value, mocks when you need to verify interactions like sending an email, and fakes when you want a simple, working substitute such as an in-memory repository. You will also learn to recognize common pitfalls: over-mocking leads to brittle tests tied to internal calls, while under-mocking can let important side effects go unverified. screens.title: What is a Test Double?
screens.narratorSegment: A test double is any object that stands in for a real object during a test. Imagine a movie set: the main actor performs the core scene while a stunt double handles the dangerous parts. In testing, the code under test is the actor and dependencies are the risky props or stunts. The double performs controlled actions so the test can focus on the actor’s behavior. This definition matters because it frames the whole purpose of replacing dependencies: to control inputs, eliminate flakiness, and make tests fast. A concrete example is an EmailService that would normally call a network A P I. A test double can prevent that call and either return a canned response, record that it was called, or act like a lightweight, in-memory email queue. A common misconception is thinking a double must perfectly mimic production behavior; in fact, doubles should be as simple as necessary to verify the behavior you care about. Over-accurate doubles add maintenance cost. The takeaway is to replace only what prevents reliable and focused testing, not to recreate the full production system inside every test.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A test double replaces a real dependency so tests can run in controlled, reliable conditions.

content.html:
Core Concept
Test Double — the stunt double for your tests
A concise definition and the movie-set analogy to ground the idea.
Analogy
Actor = code under test. Stunt double = test double handling risky or slow interactions.
When to use
When a dependency makes tests slow, flaky, or hard to set up.
Key Takeaway

Replace dependencies with doubles that give just enough control to test the behavior you care about.

Concrete example
An EmailService normally calls an external API. In tests we might use:
Stub — canned response
Returns a predefined success result so the caller proceeds without contacting the network.
Mock — records call
Asserts that send_email was called with correct arguments.
Fake — lightweight implementation
An in-memory queue that mimics email sending behavior for more complex interactions.

screens.title: Stubs: Controlled Return Values
screens.narratorSegment: A stub is a test double that returns predefined data when called. Its role is to supply the exact state or values your unit needs to proceed. Use a stub when you care about what the dependency returns, not how it was called. For example, when testing a function that builds a user profile from repository data, provide a stubbed repository that returns a concrete user object. This keeps the test deterministic and fast because it avoids real database access. Stubs are simple by design: they recite their scripted lines and do not record interactions. A common misconception is to use stubs to verify side effects; stubs do not prove that a method was called. If you need to assert that a method ran, prefer a mock. Additionally, avoid overusing stubs to recreate complex behavior — if the dependency must manage state or implement significant logic, a fake is often a better fit. The key takeaway: use stubs to control inputs and make assertions about the unit’s outputs, not to assert collaborator calls. Stubs: Controlled Return Values means a stub provides predefined answers to calls so tests can control input data and remain deterministic.. In practical terms, when you need predictable data, not interaction verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Stub
keyIdea.text: A stub provides predefined answers to calls so tests can control input data and remain deterministic.

content.html:
Definition
Stub — returns controlled data
Use when the test needs a specific return value from a dependency.
When to use
Fetching a user record to build a profile, simulating an error response, or providing a fixed timestamp.
Misconception
Stubs do not verify interactions. If you need to assert that a method was called, use a mock instead.
Key Takeaway

Choose a stub when you only need specific return values to drive the unit under test.

Concrete stub example
A repository stub returns a fixed user object so get_user_profile returns predictable data.
# Example pseudo-code for a stubbed repository
class UserRepositoryStub:
  def get_user_by_id(self, user_id):
    return {"id": user_id, "username": "alice", "email": "alice@example.com"}

# Test uses the stub rather than a real database
repo = UserRepositoryStub()
service = UserService(repo, DummyEmailService())
profile = service.get_user_profile(1)
assert profile['username'] == 'alice'
Note: the stub returns canned data and does not record calls.

screens.title: Mocks: Verifying Interactions
screens.narratorSegment: A mock is a test double that records how its methods are called so your test can verify those interactions. Use mocks when the important behavior is that a collaborator was invoked correctly — for example, sending a welcome email after registration. In such a test you assert that send_welcome_email was called once with the expected recipient and message. Mocks help confirm side effects and protocol adherence between components. One pitfall is over-reliance on mocks to assert every internal call; that creates brittle tests that fail when implementation details change but outward behavior stays correct. Contrast this with stubs: stubs provide data but do not verify calls. When you reach for a mock, ask whether the interaction is part of the unit's contract. If it is, mock it. If the interaction is incidental to the behavior, prefer asserting outcomes rather than internal call sequences. The takeaway is to use mocks to prove behavior at the unit boundary, not to lock tests to internal call order or unnecessary details. Mocks: Verifying Interactions means mocks record method calls and arguments so tests can verify that required interactions happened.. In practical terms, use mocks when the interaction with a dependency is the behavior under test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mock
keyIdea.text: Mocks record method calls and arguments so tests can verify that required interactions happened.

content.html:
Definition
Mock — verify interactions
Use mocks to assert that the unit called its collaborator correctly.
When to use
When sending notifications, logging important events, or triggering side effects is part of the behavior under test.
Misconception
Mocks should not be used to assert every internal call; focus on meaningful interactions that constitute the unit's contract.
Key Takeaway

Use mocks to verify side effects that are essential to the unit’s behavior, and avoid asserting incidental implementation details.

Concrete mock example
When registering a user, verify an EmailService mock received a call to send_welcome_email with expected args.
# Pseudo-code illustrating a mock assertion
email_mock = MockEmailService()
repo_stub = UserRepositoryStub()
service = UserService(repo_stub, email_mock)
service.register_user('alice', 'alice@example.com')
# Verify that send_welcome_email was called once with email and username
assert email_mock.assert_called_with('alice@example.com', 'alice')
Note: the mock both stands in for the service and records the call for verification.

screens.title: Fakes: Lightweight Working Implementations
screens.narratorSegment: A fake is a simplified but functional implementation of a dependency, suitable for tests but not for production. Think of an in-memory database that supports queries, inserts, and updates but stores everything in R A M. Fakes are helpful when you need more realistic interactions than a stub can provide but want to avoid the cost and complexity of a real service. Use a fake when the dependency must manage state across multiple calls or when its internal logic affects the outcome you want to test. For example, a UserRepositoryFake can accept saves and later return those entries for profile retrieval. A common misconception is believing fakes must be perfect replicas; they only need to be accurate enough for the behavior you are testing. Avoid making fakes so complex that they replicate production bugs. The takeaway: prefer fakes for richer, stateful interactions in tests while keeping them intentionally simplified and well-documented. Fakes: Lightweight Working Implementations means a fake is a working, simplified implementation used when stateful or multi-step behavior is necessary for tests.. In practical terms, when behavior and state matter but production overhead is unnecessary. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fake
keyIdea.text: A fake is a working, simplified implementation used when stateful or multi-step behavior is necessary for tests.

content.html:
Definition
Fake — simplified, working substitute
Use when the dependency must maintain state or provide multi-step behavior in a test-friendly way.
When to use
In-memory databases, simple queues, or lightweight caches used in tests for richer scenarios.
Misconception
Fakes should not recreate production complexity; make them simple and focused on test needs.
Key Takeaway

Use fakes when tests require stateful or multi-step interactions that stubs cannot provide.

Concrete fake example
An in-memory repository that implements save and get operations for test scenarios.
# Pseudo-code for a simple in-memory fake
class InMemoryUserRepo:
  def __init__(self):
    self._store = {}
  def save_user(self, user_data):
    self._store[user_data['id']] = user_data
  def get_user_by_id(self, user_id):
    return self._store.get(user_id)

# Tests can save then fetch within the same test run without external DB
Keep the fake small and well-documented to avoid hidden test complexity.

screens.title: Choosing the Right Test Double
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting the correct test double depends on what you want to verify. Start by asking: do I care about the data returned, the interaction, or the dependency’s internal behavior? If you care only about returned data, choose a stub. If you care that the unit invoked a collaborator correctly, choose a mock. If you need stateful behavior across calls, choose a fake. An example decision flow: when testing get_user_profile, you want a specific user object, so use a stub that returns that object. When testing register_user, you want to verify the repository saved the user and an email was sent, so use mocks for those interactions. If your repository must support multi-step queries during the same test, use a fake in-memory repository. A common error is to reflexively mock every dependency; instead, match the double to the test's goal. This keeps tests maintainable and focused. The takeaway is to consistently ask "data, interaction, or behavior?" and let that answer pick your double. Choosing the Right Test Double means ask whether the test cares about data, interactions, or stateful behavior — then choose stub, mock, or fake accordingly.. In practical terms, a simple decision process to select stub, mock, or fake. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decision guide
keyIdea.text: Ask whether the test cares about data, interactions, or stateful behavior — then choose stub, mock, or fake accordingly.

content.html:
Process Flow
Decide: Data, Interaction, or State
1. Do you need a specific return value?
Yes → Stub. No → go to 2.
2. Do you need to verify a call or arguments?
Yes → Mock. No → go to 3.
3. Is state or multi-call behavior required?
Yes → Fake. Otherwise prefer simple stubs or small integration tests.
Misconception: Choosing based on what’s easiest to implement rather than what the test needs leads to brittle suites.
Concrete scenarios
get_user_profile → Stub
We only need a controlled user object to verify returned profile fields.
register_user → Mock
We must assert that save and send_welcome_email were called with correct arguments.
Complex repository flows → Fake
Use an in-memory fake when multiple operations must interact with the same state.
Pro tip

Start with the simplest double that gives clear, focused assertions. Only add complexity when tests demand it.

screens.title: Hands-on: UserService Example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the UserService example from the chapter to make choices concrete. The UserService depends on a UserRepository and an EmailService. For register_user, the method saves a user to the repository and then sends a welcome email. Because register_user's correctness includes those side effects, our tests should verify the interactions: we want to assert that save_user and send_welcome_email were invoked with correct arguments. That makes mocks the appropriate double for both dependencies in a pure unit test. For get_user_profile, we only care that the repository returns a user object and that the service returns it unchanged; the test cares about returned data, so a stubbed repository that returns a predefined user is ideal. If register_user required more realistic repository behavior — for instance generating incremental IDs or enforcing constraints — an in-memory fake repository could be used instead. A common mistaken pattern is to mock everything: this can hide integration errors and produce brittle tests. Prefer stubs and fakes where behavior or returned data is the focus, and reserve mocks for interactions that are part of the unit’s contract.

keyIdea.title: UserService decisions
keyIdea.text: Mocks for interaction verification in register_user; stub for data return in get_user_profile; fake when richer state is required.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
UserService dependencies and choices
Identify direct dependencies and match doubles to the test goal.
Dependencies
UserRepository — data store. EmailService — notification side effect.
Decision
register_user: mocks to verify save and send calls. get_user_profile: stub to return a known user.
Key Takeaway

Match the double to whether you test for return values, interactions, or richer stateful behavior.

Conceptual Python-like code (illustrative)
# user_service.py (Conceptual - no implementation yet)

class UserRepository:
    def get_user_by_id(self, user_id: int):
        # Imagine this makes a database call
        raise NotImplementedError("Database interaction not implemented")

    def save_user(self, user_data: dict):
        # Imagine this saves to a database
        raise NotImplementedError("Database interaction not implemented")

class EmailService:
    def send_welcome_email(self, user_email: str, username: str):
        # Imagine this makes an API call to an email provider
        print(f"Sending welcome email to {user_email} for {username}")

class UserService:
    def __init__(self, user_repo: UserRepository, email_service: EmailService):
        self.user_repo = user_repo
        self.email_service = email_service

    def register_user(self, username: str, email: str) -> dict:

screens.title: Stubs vs Mocks vs Fakes
screens.narratorSegment: It's easy to conflate stubs, mocks, and fakes if you only read short definitions. A side-by-side comparison helps. Stubs are simple data providers: they return pre-programmed values and do not record calls. Mocks replace collaborators and record interactions so you can assert that expected calls happened. Fakes are lightweight functioning implementations that provide realistic behavior for multi-step or stateful flows. Each has a clear use case: stubs for deterministic inputs, mocks for verifying side effects, and fakes for richer in-test behavior. A typical confusion arises when learners use mocks everywhere because they can always assert calls — this produces brittle tests tied to internals. Conversely, relying solely on stubs can let important side effects go untested. The practical rule: choose the minimal double that proves the behavior you care about. If you need both return values and interaction checks, combine doubles judiciously, keeping each test focused and easy to reason about. Stubs vs Mocks vs Fakes means stubs provide data, mocks verify calls, and fakes implement simplified behavior — pick the right one based on the test’s purpose.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Stub
Provides predefined data
Returns canned responses so tests can verify outputs deterministically.
Not for verifying calls.
Mock
Records interactions
Use to assert that methods were called with expected arguments.
Avoid asserting unnecessary internal calls.
Fake
Simplified working implementation
Good for stateful behavior and multi-step interactions without external systems.
Keep fakes intentionally small.
Practical rule

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Anti-patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Test doubles improve tests, but misused they create maintenance burdens. One common pitfall is over-mocking: verifying internal call sequences that are not part of the unit's public contract. This leads to brittle tests that break when refactoring internal implementation, even though behavior is unchanged. Another pitfall is creating fakes that are too complex — essentially reimplementing production logic in test code, which duplicates bugs and increases maintenance. Under-mocking is also a danger: failing to verify an essential interaction can let regressions slip through. A frequent beginner error is using a stub where a mock is required to ensure a side effect occurs, such as sending a payment confirmation. To avoid these issues, design tests around observable behavior and unit boundaries. Use integration tests to validate full interactions with real systems, and use unit tests with minimal doubles to verify local logic. The takeaway: use doubles deliberately and document their intended scope so the test suite remains robust and understandable. Tests that assert every internal call become brittle. Focus on public contract and essential interactions.
Example

fullNarratorScript:
In real systems your units rarely operate alone. When code under test depends on databases, networks, or third-party APIs, tests can become slow, flaky, or difficult to set up. Test doubles are a practical solution: lightweight stand-ins that let you control behavior and isolate the unit you want to verify. In this lesson you will learn the difference between data-focused doubles and interaction-focused doubles, and when to use an in-memory lightweight implementation. We will use a simple UserService example throughout — saving a user and sending a welcome email — so you can see concrete choices for each dependency. You will also learn common mistakes such as over-mocking and brittle verification, and how to choose the minimal double that gives you confidence without coupling tests to implementation details. By the end you will be able to pick between a stub, a mock, and a fake based on whether you care about the returned data, the interactions, or the dependency’s behavior.

In this first objectives panel we set clear, practical outcomes. First, you will explain the core problem that test doubles solve: dependencies make unit tests slow, brittle, or hard to set up, so doubles let you control and isolate behavior. Second, you'll differentiate between real dependencies and test doubles, learning the vocabulary so you can name what you replace and why. Third, you'll identify the core characteristics and use cases for stubs, mocks, and fakes — knowing when you need data, when you must assert an interaction, and when a lightweight implementation is appropriate. Fourth, you will understand the importance of test isolation: how keeping a single unit accountable prevents unrelated failures from cascading. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or visual cue so you remember whether you're testing for data, behavior, or behavior with simplified functionality.

This second objectives panel focuses on doing and avoiding mistakes. You will practice selecting the right double for a concrete example: a UserService that saves users and sends welcome emails. You will learn to choose stubs when a method must return a controlled value, mocks when you need to verify interactions like sending an email, and fakes when you want a simple, working substitute such as an in-memory repository. You will also learn to recognize common pitfalls: over-mocking leads to brittle tests tied to internal calls, while under-mocking can let important side effects go unverified. Finally, you'll learn one assessment strategy: present a scenario and justify the double choice, so you can explain both the technical reason and the test outcome you expect. Learning Objectives — Practice & Pitfalls means practice choosing doubles for real code and recognize common pitfalls like over-mocking and brittle verification.. In practical terms, applying and avoiding mistakes with test doubles. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A test double is any object that stands in for a real object during a test. Imagine a movie set: the main actor performs the core scene while a stunt double handles the dangerous parts. In testing, the code under test is the actor and dependencies are the risky props or stunts. The double performs controlled actions so the test can focus on the actor’s behavior. This definition matters because it frames the whole purpose of replacing dependencies: to control inputs, eliminate flakiness, and make tests fast. A concrete example is an EmailService that would normally call a network A P I. A test double can prevent that call and either return a canned response, record that it was called, or act like a lightweight, in-memory email queue. A common misconception is thinking a double must perfectly mimic production behavior; in fact, doubles should be as simple as necessary to verify the behavior you care about. Over-accurate doubles add maintenance cost. The takeaway is to replace only what prevents reliable and focused testing, not to recreate the full production system inside every test.

A stub is a test double that returns predefined data when called. Its role is to supply the exact state or values your unit needs to proceed. Use a stub when you care about what the dependency returns, not how it was called. For example, when testing a function that builds a user profile from repository data, provide a stubbed repository that returns a concrete user object. This keeps the test deterministic and fast because it avoids real database access. Stubs are simple by design: they recite their scripted lines and do not record interactions. A common misconception is to use stubs to verify side effects; stubs do not prove that a method was called. If you need to assert that a method ran, prefer a mock. Additionally, avoid overusing stubs to recreate complex behavior — if the dependency must manage state or implement significant logic, a fake is often a better fit. The key takeaway: use stubs to control inputs and make assertions about the unit’s outputs, not to assert collaborator calls. Stubs: Controlled Return Values means a stub provides predefined answers to calls so tests can control input data and remain deterministic.. In practical terms, when you need predictable data, not interaction verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A mock is a test double that records how its methods are called so your test can verify those interactions. Use mocks when the important behavior is that a collaborator was invoked correctly — for example, sending a welcome email after registration. In such a test you assert that send_welcome_email was called once with the expected recipient and message. Mocks help confirm side effects and protocol adherence between components. One pitfall is over-reliance on mocks to assert every internal call; that creates brittle tests that fail when implementation details change but outward behavior stays correct. Contrast this with stubs: stubs provide data but do not verify calls. When you reach for a mock, ask whether the interaction is part of the unit's contract. If it is, mock it. If the interaction is incidental to the behavior, prefer asserting outcomes rather than internal call sequences. The takeaway is to use mocks to prove behavior at the unit boundary, not to lock tests to internal call order or unnecessary details. Mocks: Verifying Interactions means mocks record method calls and arguments so tests can verify that required interactions happened.. In practical terms, use mocks when the interaction with a dependency is the behavior under test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A fake is a simplified but functional implementation of a dependency, suitable for tests but not for production. Think of an in-memory database that supports queries, inserts, and updates but stores everything in R A M. Fakes are helpful when you need more realistic interactions than a stub can provide but want to avoid the cost and complexity of a real service. Use a fake when the dependency must manage state across multiple calls or when its internal logic affects the outcome you want to test. For example, a UserRepositoryFake can accept saves and later return those entries for profile retrieval. A common misconception is believing fakes must be perfect replicas; they only need to be accurate enough for the behavior you are testing. Avoid making fakes so complex that they replicate production bugs. The takeaway: prefer fakes for richer, stateful interactions in tests while keeping them intentionally simplified and well-documented. Fakes: Lightweight Working Implementations means a fake is a working, simplified implementation used when stateful or multi-step behavior is necessary for tests.. In practical terms, when behavior and state matter but production overhead is unnecessary. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Selecting the correct test double depends on what you want to verify. Start by asking: do I care about the data returned, the interaction, or the dependency’s internal behavior? If you care only about returned data, choose a stub. If you care that the unit invoked a collaborator correctly, choose a mock. If you need stateful behavior across calls, choose a fake. An example decision flow: when testing get_user_profile, you want a specific user object, so use a stub that returns that object. When testing register_user, you want to verify the repository saved the user and an email was sent, so use mocks for those interactions. If your repository must support multi-step queries during the same test, use a fake in-memory repository. A common error is to reflexively mock every dependency; instead, match the double to the test's goal. This keeps tests maintainable and focused. The takeaway is to consistently ask "data, interaction, or behavior?" and let that answer pick your double. Choosing the Right Test Double means ask whether the test cares about data, interactions, or stateful behavior — then choose stub, mock, or fake accordingly.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

For register_user, the method saves a user to the repository and then sends a welcome email. Because register_user's correctness includes those side effects, our tests should verify the interactions: we want to assert that save_user and send_welcome_email were invoked with correct arguments. That makes mocks the appropriate double for both dependencies in a pure unit test. For get_user_profile, we only care that the repository returns a user object and that the service returns it unchanged; the test cares about returned data, so a stubbed repository that returns a predefined user is ideal. If register_user required more realistic repository behavior — for instance generating incremental IDs or enforcing constraints — an in-memory fake repository could be used instead. A common mistaken pattern is to mock everything: this can hide integration errors and produce brittle tests. Prefer stubs and fakes where behavior or returned data is the focus, and reserve mocks for interactions that are part of the unit’s contract.

This leads to brittle tests that break when refactoring internal implementation, even though behavior is unchanged. Another pitfall is creating fakes that are too complex — essentially reimplementing production logic in test code, which duplicates bugs and increases maintenance. Under-mocking is also a danger: failing to verify an essential interaction can let regressions slip through. A frequent beginner error is using a stub where a mock is required to ensure a side effect occurs, such as sending a payment confirmation. To avoid these issues, design tests around observable behavior and unit boundaries. Use integration tests to validate full interactions with real systems, and use unit tests with minimal doubles to verify local logic. The takeaway: use doubles deliberately and document their intended scope so the test suite remains robust and understandable. Summarize and lock in three essential ideas. First, a test double is any object that stands in for a real dependency to keep tests focused and reliable. Second, choose your double by asking whether the test cares about returned data, the interaction, or stateful behavior: stubs for data, mocks for interactions, and fakes for simplified working behavior. Third, be mindful of pitfalls: over-mocking produces brittle tests, and over-complex fakes duplicate production logic. Use the simplest double that proves the behavior under test and reserve integration tests for verifying production interactions. These three reminders help keep your test suite fast, clear, and maintainable. Keep these quick reference cards handy as you write tests. First, if your test needs a specific return value to exercise logic, prefer a stub. Second, if the behavior you care about is that the unit invoked a collaborator with certain arguments, prefer a mock. Third, if tests require stateful or multi-step behavior, use a fake — but keep it intentionally simpler than production. When in doubt, document the assumption your double encodes and ask whether an integration test should validate the real interaction.
